# 15 Halogen compounds

本章只覆盖 AS 3.3 Halogen Compounds 中的 **15.1 Halogenoalkanes**。题目使用 AS 原题包中的原文，不改写题干；可独立提取的结构式、流程图、曲线图和装置图保留为独立图像。无法独立提取的整页图片不放入页面。

## Learning objectives

- identify primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes;
- explain nucleophilic substitution and distinguish S<sub>N</sub>1/S<sub>N</sub>2;
- predict products with OH<sup>−</sup>, CN<sup>−</sup> and NH<sub>3</sub>;
- use silver nitrate to compare halogenoalkane hydrolysis;
- explain the stability and environmental impact of CFCs.

## 15.1 Halogenoalkanes and the C–X bond

A halogenoalkane has a halogen attached to an alkyl group, R–X. The carbon bonded to the halogen is δ<sup>+</sup> because halogen is more electronegative; it is attacked by nucleophiles. A **primary** halogenoalkane has the C–X carbon bonded to one other carbon, a secondary to two, and a tertiary to three.

The C–X bond strength decreases down the group: C–F > C–Cl > C–Br > C–I. Thus iodoalkanes hydrolyse fastest and chloroalkanes slowest (among Cl, Br and I). In warm ethanol/water with aqueous AgNO<sub>3</sub>, released halide gives AgCl white, AgBr cream, or AgI yellow precipitate. The rate follows RI > RBr > RCl because less bond energy is needed to break C–I.

### Core diagrams from the original 15.1 Note

The following independent diagrams are re-extracted from the original Note PDF and composited onto a white background. They summarise the three classes of halogenoalkane and the polarity of the C–X bond.

![Classification of primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes](../assets/notes/halogenoalkanes-rebuilt/halogenoalkanes-img-031.png){.concept-figure fig-alt="Primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes"}

![Polarity of the carbon–halogen bond](../assets/notes/halogenoalkanes-rebuilt/halogenoalkanes-img-037.png){.concept-figure fig-alt="Partial charges and polarity of the C-X bond"}

The carbon atom is δ<sup>+</sup> and can be attacked by a nucleophile. When halogenoalkanes are prepared from alkenes, HX undergoes electrophilic addition; the more stable carbocation pathway gives the major product.

![Electrophilic addition of hydrogen halide or halogen](../assets/notes/halogenoalkanes-rebuilt/halogenoalkanes-img-013.png){.concept-figure fig-alt="Electrophilic addition to alkenes forming halogenoalkanes"}

## 15.2 Nucleophilic substitution

Nucleophiles donate a lone pair to the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon and replace X<sup>−</sup>. Aqueous OH<sup>−</sup> gives an alcohol; ethanolic CN<sup>−</sup> gives a nitrile; excess ethanolic NH<sub>3</sub> under pressure gives an amine.

<div class="equation-block">R–Br + OH<sup>−</sup> → R–OH + Br<sup>−</sup><br>R–Br + CN<sup>−</sup> → R–CN + Br<sup>−</sup><br>R–Br + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → R–NH<sub>2</sub> + NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + Br<sup>−</sup></div>

Using CN<sup>−</sup> is valuable because it adds one carbon atom to the chain. Acid hydrolysis of the nitrile then gives a carboxylic acid.

Primary halogenoalkanes normally react by **S<sub>N</sub>2**: one concerted step, with nucleophile attack and C–X breaking simultaneously; the rate depends on both halogenoalkane and nucleophile. Tertiary halogenoalkanes usually react by **S<sub>N</sub>1**: slow heterolytic C–X fission makes a carbocation, then rapid nucleophile attack; the rate depends only on halogenoalkane concentration.

## 15.3 Elimination and preparation

Hot ethanolic OH<sup>−</sup> promotes elimination: H and X are removed from adjacent atoms to form C=C, for example CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + OH<sup>−</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + Br<sup>−</sup>. Aqueous OH<sup>−</sup> instead favours substitution. Halogenoalkanes are also formed by free-radical substitution of alkanes with Cl<sub>2</sub>/UV, and by electrophilic addition of HX or X<sub>2</sub> to alkenes.

![Free-radical substitution of ethane by chlorine](../assets/notes/halogenoalkanes-rebuilt/halogenoalkanes-img-008.png){.concept-figure fig-alt="Initiation, propagation and termination in free-radical substitution"}

## 15.4 CFCs and ozone depletion

CFCs were useful as refrigerants and propellants because they are inert, non-flammable and non-toxic at ground level. Strong C–F bonds help their stability. Their long lifetime lets them diffuse to the stratosphere, where UV radiation causes homolytic bond fission and releases chlorine radicals.

<div class="equation-block">CCl<sub>2</sub>F<sub>2</sub> → CClF<sub>2</sub>· + Cl·<br>Cl· + O<sub>3</sub> → ClO· + O<sub>2</sub><br>ClO· + O → Cl· + O<sub>2</sub></div>

Chlorine radical is regenerated, so one radical can catalyse the destruction of many ozone molecules. Ozone normally absorbs harmful UV radiation; CFC manufacture has therefore been phased out under the Montreal Protocol.

### Question 1 · 3.3 SQ Easy Q1(a-d)
<img src="../assets/questions/extracted/15/rebuilt/sq-easy-q1-fig-1-1.png" class="question-figure" alt="Displayed formula of a bromoalkane">
![Fig. 1.2 Structure of the corresponding chloroalkane](../assets/questions/extracted/15/rebuilt/sq-easy-q1-fig-1-2.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Displayed formula of the corresponding chloroalkane"}
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> Name the compound shown in Fig. 1.1.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> State the class of halogenoalkane to which this compound belongs.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> State the colour of the precipitate formed in the reaction between the halogenoalkane in Fig. 1.1 and acidified silver nitrate, AgNO<sub>3</sub>.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> The compound drawn in Fig. 1.1 is reacted with alcoholic potassium cyanide, KCN. The reaction is heated under reflux. Draw the product of this nucleophilic substitution reaction.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> The halogenoalkane drawn in Fig. 1.2 contains a chlorine atom instead of a bromine atom. This halogenoalkane is reacted under the same conditions outlined in part (c). Briefly explain why the reaction with the bromine-containing halogenoalkane would be faster.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>The compound is 2-bromopropane, a secondary halogenoalkane.</li><li>The precipitate is cream AgBr.</li><li>CN<sup>−</sup> replaces Br<sup>−</sup>, giving butanenitrile, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CN.</li><li>The C–Br bond is weaker than the C–Cl bond, so it breaks more readily and the substitution is faster.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-02}
### Question 2 · 3.3 SQ Easy Q2(a-c)
<p>Fig. 2.1 shows the reaction profile for the production of propene: propane → 1-chloropropane → propene.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> State the conditions required for step 1.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> Name the mechanism for step 1.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> The mechanism for step 1 involves initiation, propagation and termination. Write both missing propagation equations.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> Name the mechanism for step 2.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> State the reagent and necessary conditions for step 2.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>Use Cl<sub>2</sub> and UV light; step 1 is free-radical substitution.</li><li>Cl· + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> → HCl + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>·; CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>· + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + Cl·.</li><li>Step 2 is elimination; use concentrated ethanolic NaOH or KOH and heat under reflux.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-03}
### Question 3 · 3.3 SQ Easy Q3(a-c)
<img src="../assets/questions/extracted/15/rebuilt/sq-easy-q3-fig-3-1.png" class="question-figure" alt="Incomplete two-step SN1 mechanism for 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with hydroxide ions">
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> State what is meant by the term tertiary halogenoalkane.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism, whereas primary halogenoalkanes react via an S<sub>N</sub>2 mechanism. Explain what the numbers 1 and 2 refer to in S<sub>N</sub>1 and S<sub>N</sub>2.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with hydroxide ions via an S<sub>N</sub>1 mechanism. Complete the reaction mechanism shown in Fig. 3.1, clearly showing partial charges, full charges and the transfer of electrons.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> Identify which, step 1 or step 2, is the rate-determining step.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> An ethanolic solution of excess ammonia is heated under pressure with 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Draw the structure of the resulting organic product.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> State the name of the functional group of the organic product.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>A tertiary halogenoalkane has the carbon bonded to the halogen attached to three other carbon atoms.</li><li>The number gives the number of reacting species in the rate-determining step: one for S<sub>N</sub>1 and two for S<sub>N</sub>2.</li><li>Step 1 is heterolytic C–Br fission to form a tertiary carbocation and Br<sup>−</sup>; step 2 is attack by OH<sup>−</sup>. Step 1 is rate determining.</li><li>The product is 2-methylpropan-2-amine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CNH<sub>2</sub>, containing an amine functional group.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-04}
### Question 4 · 3.3 SQ Medium Q1(a-e)
<p>The molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> represents propene and cyclopropane, shown in Fig. 1.1.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> What is the H–C–H bond angle at the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> group in propene?</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> Under suitable conditions, propene and cyclopropane each react with chlorine. With propene, 1,2-dichloropropane, CH<sub>3</sub>CHClCH<sub>2</sub>Cl, is formed. State fully what type of reaction this is.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> When cyclopropane reacts with chlorine, three different compounds with molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> can be formed. Draw displayed structures of each of these three compounds.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> Ethane reacts with chlorine according to C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + HCl. State the conditions needed.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> State the type of reaction occurring here.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(i)</strong> Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate the enthalpy change for Cl· + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> → HCl + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>·. Show your working.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(ii)</strong> Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate the enthalpy change for I· + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> → HI + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>·. Show your working.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(iii)</strong> Hence suggest why it is not possible to make iodoethane by reacting iodine and ethane.</p>
<p><strong>(e)</strong> Complete the equations of some possible steps in the formation of chloroethane.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>The terminal carbon is sp<sup>2</sup>; the angle is 120°.</li><li>Propene + chlorine is electrophilic addition. Cyclopropane gives the three displayed C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> structures from addition/substitution at the ring.</li><li>Use chlorine and UV light; the reaction is free-radical substitution.</li><li>Calculate ΔH from bonds broken minus bonds formed. The iodine abstraction step is endothermic, so the chain is not sustained and iodoethane is not formed.</li><li>For propagation, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>· + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl + Cl·; termination combines radicals.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-05}
### Question 5 · 3.3 SQ Medium Q2(a-e)
![Fig. 2.1 Reaction scheme from 1-chloropropane](../assets/questions/extracted/15/rebuilt/sq-medium-q2-fig-2-1.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Reaction scheme showing 1-chloropropane forming propene, butanenitrile and propan-1-amine"}
![Fig. 2.2 Concentration-time graph](../assets/questions/extracted/15/rebuilt/sq-medium-q2-fig-2-2.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Concentration of a tertiary chloroalkane plotted against time"}
<p>1-chloropropane can react to form organic products as shown in the reaction scheme in Fig. 2.1.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> State the reagent and conditions used in Reaction 1.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> Identify a suitable reagent for Reaction 2 and include a reason why this is a particularly useful type of reaction in organic chemistry.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(iii)</strong> State the conditions used in Reaction 3.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(iv)</strong> Write the structural formula of the product formed if 1-chloropropane is refluxed with aqueous sodium hydroxide.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> 2-chloro-2-methylpropane reacts with aqueous alkali to form 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Use the concentration–time graph in Fig. 2.2 to calculate the rate of reaction at 50 s. Show your working and include units.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> What is the classification of the mechanism for this reaction?</p>
<p><strong>(d)(i)</strong> State the visible change when 1-bromobutane is added to ethanol and aqueous silver nitrate. Include the formula of the compound responsible.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(ii)</strong> State the order of decreasing rate for 1-bromobutane, 1-iodobutane and 1-chlorobutane.</p>
<p><strong>(e)</strong> 2-bromo-2-methylpropane can be prepared by addition of HBr to 2-methylpropene. Draw the mechanism, including curly arrows, relevant dipoles and lone pairs.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>Reaction 1: hot ethanolic NaOH/KOH and elimination. Reaction 2: ethanolic KCN under reflux; it adds one carbon and is useful for chain extension. Reaction 3: excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure and heat. Aqueous NaOH gives propan-1-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH.</li><li>Use the tangent gradient at 50 s; report the rate in mol dm<sup>−3</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>.</li><li>S<sub>N</sub>1.</li><li>AgBr is a cream precipitate; the rate order is 1-iodobutane &gt; 1-bromobutane &gt; 1-chlorobutane.</li><li>Show electrophilic addition through the tertiary carbocation, followed by Br<sup>−</sup> attack.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-06}
### Question 6 · 3.3 SQ Hard Q1(a-d)
<p>This question is about halogenoalkanes. A student investigates the rate of reaction of six halogenoalkanes using the method and results in Table 1.1.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> Suggest how the student could improve the method.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> Other than precipitation, state what type of reaction is occurring in this method.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Using Table 1.1, describe and explain two factors that influence the rate of this type of reaction in halogenoalkanes.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> A fresh sample of aqueous 1-bromopentane reacts with an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide. Fully identify the mechanism for this reaction and state the number of steps in the mechanism.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> One of the products contains bromine. Name this product.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(iii)</strong> The reaction conditions are changed, resulting in the formation of three products, including the product identified in part (c)(ii). Suggest the change made to the conditions.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(i)</strong> 1-chloropentane was prepared by reaction of an alcohol and thionyl chloride, SOCl<sub>2</sub>. Give the equation, including state symbols.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(ii)</strong> Explain one necessary safety precaution and justify your answer.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>Use equal measured volumes of ethanol, halogenoalkane and AgNO<sub>3</sub>; pre-equilibrate all reactants at 50 °C; use a thermostated bath and repeat measurements. The organic reaction is hydrolysis/nucleophilic substitution.</li><li>Iodoalkanes react fastest because C–I is weakest; tertiary/branched halogenoalkanes react faster in S<sub>N</sub>1 because they form more stable carbocations.</li><li>Aqueous 1-bromopentane reacts by S<sub>N</sub>2 in one step; the bromine-containing product is NaBr. Ethanolic NaOH permits competing elimination and gives three products overall.</li><li>CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>OH(l) + SOCl<sub>2</sub>(l) → CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl(l) + SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + HCl(g). Use a fume cupboard because toxic/acidic gases are evolved.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-07}
### Question 7 · 3.3 SQ Hard Q2(a-d)
<p>2-bromo-2-methylpropane is refluxed with ethanolic potassium hydroxide, KOH. The result is a mixture of products containing roughly a 4:1 ratio of alkene to alcohol.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Complete Table 2.1 to name the organic products and identify the mechanisms involved.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Suggest why there is a mixture of an alkene and an alcohol produced in the reaction outlined in part (a).</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Give the equation for the reaction between butan-2-ol and phosphorus(III) iodide.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Explain why sulfuric acid cannot be used in the preparation of an iodoalkane.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>The alkene is 2-methylpropene from elimination; the alcohol is 2-methylpropan-2-ol from nucleophilic substitution.</li><li>Ethanolic OH<sup>−</sup> favours elimination, but nucleophilic substitution also occurs.</li><li>3CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + PI<sub>3</sub> → 3CH<sub>3</sub>CH(I)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub>.</li><li>Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> oxidises I<sup>−</sup>/HI to iodine, so it cannot be used simply to generate HI.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-08}
### Question 8 · 3.3 SQ Hard Q3(a-c)
<img src="../assets/questions/extracted/15/rebuilt/sq-hard-q3-fig-3-1.png" class="question-figure" alt="Reaction scheme showing compound G forming compound H and a nitrile">
<p>Compound G is a chloroalkane that can undergo two different reactions as outlined in Fig. 3.1. Compound H is an alkene which does not exhibit geometric isomerism.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Draw the skeletal structures of compounds G and H.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> State the reagents and conditions required for reaction A.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Name and draw the mechanism for reaction B. Include all charges, partial charges, lone pairs and curly arrows.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>Draw the matching chloroalkane G and the alkene H in which one carbon of C=C has two identical groups, so no E/Z isomerism is possible.</li><li>Use hot ethanolic NaOH/KOH for elimination.</li><li>Reaction B is nucleophilic substitution: CN<sup>−</sup> attacks the δ+ carbon and the C–Cl bond electrons move to Cl<sup>−</sup>. Use KCN in ethanol under reflux.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-09}
### Question 9 · 3.3 SQ Hard Q4(a-f)
![Apparatus for producing and collecting gaseous butenes](../assets/questions/extracted/15/rebuilt/sq-hard-q4-apparatus.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Gas syringe and reflux condenser apparatus for producing gaseous butenes"}
<p>Bromobutanes react with hot ethanolic potassium hydroxide solution to produce gaseous butenes. In the experiment, 0.0080 mol of liquid 1-bromobutane is injected into hot ethanolic KOH and 22.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of but-1-ene is collected after cooling to 25 °C.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> State the purpose of the condenser.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Describe a chemical test and the expected observation to identify the functional group of the gas.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Calculate the percentage of 1-bromobutane converted to but-1-ene.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Before cooling, the volume of but-1-ene in the gas syringe was 24.0 cm<sup>3</sup>. Assuming constant pressure and no loss of but-1-ene, calculate the temperature of the gas before cooling.</p>
<p><strong>(e)(i)</strong> Another compound formed from 1-bromobutane under these conditions is butan-1-ol. Fully identify the type of reaction taking place.</p>
<p><strong>(e)(ii)</strong> Draw the mechanism for the reaction of 1-bromobutane with hydroxide ions to form butan-1-ol. Include charges, partial charges, lone pairs and curly arrows.</p>
<p><strong>(e)(iii)</strong> Describe a chemical test and the expected observations to confirm the presence of the functional group in butan-1-ol.</p>
<p><strong>(f)</strong> Isomeric alkene molecules are formed in the elimination reaction of 2-bromobutane. Draw the displayed formulae of the isomers formed.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>The condenser prevents volatile reactants/ethanol escaping during reflux.</li><li>Bromine water is decolourised, confirming a C=C bond.</li><li>Use n = pV/RT for 22.0 cm<sup>3</sup> at 25 °C, divide by 0.0080 mol and multiply by 100.</li><li>At constant pressure, V<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>, so use 24.0 cm<sup>3</sup> and 22.0 cm<sup>3</sup> with 298 K.</li><li>Formation of butan-1-ol is nucleophilic substitution by OH<sup>−</sup>; acidified dichromate changes orange to green on warming for a primary alcohol.</li><li>The alkene isomers are but-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hal-sq-10}
### Question 10 · 3.3 SQ Medium Q3(a-d)
![Fig. 3.1 Reaction scheme for 1-bromobutane](../assets/questions/extracted/15/rebuilt/sq-medium-q3-fig-3-1.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Reaction scheme showing reactions of 1-bromobutane with aqueous and ethanolic sodium hydroxide"}
<p>One method of making 1-bromobutane in the laboratory uses powdered potassium bromide, water, butan-1-ol and concentrated sulfuric acid.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Write an equation for each of the two stages: formation of HBr, and reaction of butan-1-ol with HBr.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> State two different ways that 1-bromobutane can be prepared. Include the reagents and conditions.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> Complete the reaction scheme starting with 1-bromobutane. In each empty box, write the structural formula of the organic compound formed.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> State the name of the type of reaction that occurs when X is produced from 1-bromobutane.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Compound W can also be formed from 1-bromobutane by heating it under reflux with aqueous silver nitrate. Suggest why formation of W is slower than when aqueous sodium hydroxide is used.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>KBr + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → KHSO<sub>4</sub> + HBr; CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>OH + HBr → CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>Br + H<sub>2</sub>O.</li><li>Valid alternatives include butan-1-ol with PBr<sub>3</sub>, or a suitable precursor with HBr under appropriate conditions.</li><li>Aqueous OH<sup>−</sup> gives butan-1-ol, which can be oxidised to butanoic acid; ethanolic OH<sup>−</sup> gives but-1-ene and oxidation cleaves the C=C.</li><li>Water is a weaker nucleophile than OH<sup>−</sup>, so hydrolysis is slower with aqueous AgNO<sub>3</sub>.</li></ul></details>
:::
